name: Sales, Use and Value Added Tax
title: Sales, Use and Value Added Tax
answer: Sales, use and value added tax covers the indirect taxes charged on goods and services as they move through a supply chain. Sales tax applies at retail in state and local jurisdictions, use tax complements it on out-of-state purchases where sales tax was not collected, and value added tax applies at each stage of production and distribution in many countries. The scope includes determining taxability, rates, exemptions, nexus, and filing obligations across borders. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages track many of these rules and their updates.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on transaction data from billing, ERP, and point-of-sale systems, fed into tax engines that hold jurisdiction boundaries, rate tables, and product taxability rules. Common platforms include Avalara, Vertex, and Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE, alongside exemption certificate management tools and e-invoicing networks. These systems connect to general ledgers and reporting suites so that calculated tax can be posted, reconciled, and remitted. Data quality depends on clean product master data and accurate customer location information.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by mapping nexus, which means where a business has enough presence to be required to collect tax. They then classify each product or service, apply the correct rate and exemption, and calculate tax on invoices. For VAT, the work includes input tax credits, reverse charges, and cross-border rules. Returns are prepared, reconciled against ledger balances, and filed on a schedule that varies by jurisdiction. Automation and AI tools are increasingly used for classification, anomaly detection, and audit trail review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The legal basis for these taxes sits in statutes, regulations, and case law, and the burden of proof generally falls on the taxpayer to show that a position is correct. Risks include misclassification, missed exemptions, incorrect rates, and penalties or interest on assessment. Provenance matters because auditors will ask for transaction records, exemption certificates, and a clear audit trail from source data to filed return. The site's 686 glossary terms include definitions for concepts such as nexus, reverse charge, and place of supply.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Jurisdictions are moving toward real-time or near-real-time reporting, with e-invoicing mandates and continuous transaction controls expanding in many regions. Digital services taxes and post-Wayfair nexus rules continue to add complexity for cross-border sellers. AI is being applied to tax determination, risk scoring, and document review, though human review remains standard for filing positions. The direction is toward more granular data, more frequent filing, and tighter integration between tax engines and core financial systems.
